To outflank someone means to go around their side in order to gain an advantage over them — whether on a real battlefield or in any competitive situation in life.

The key idea is this: instead of attacking or confronting someone directly from the front, you move cleverly around their side so that you end up in a stronger position than them. It always involves strategy, movement, and outsmarting someone.

The word contains the word "flank" within it. The flank of anything — an army, an animal, a building — simply means its side. Your flanks are your sides, the areas to your left and right.

So "out-flank" = to go beyond someone's flank = to get around their side and past them.

This word was born on the battlefield, and understanding this image will lock the meaning in your mind forever.

Imagine two armies facing each other. Army A is on one side, Army B is on the other. Both armies are prepared to defend against a frontal attack — a straight-on charge from the enemy directly in front of them. Their shields, their guns, their strongest soldiers — all facing forward.

Now, Army A decides not to attack from the front. Instead, they quietly send a large group of soldiers around the side of Army B, curving around them. Suddenly, Army B finds enemy soldiers attacking them from the side or even from behind — directions they weren't prepared for. They are now surrounded, confused, and vulnerable.

Army A has just outflanked Army B.

This was one of the most effective and feared tactics in military history. Generals like Alexander the Great and Napoleon built entire reputations on outflanking their enemies.

Example:

"The general outflanked the enemy by sending his cavalry through the forest to attack from the rear."

Today, most people use "outflank" outside of war entirely. It has moved into business, politics, arguments, sports, and everyday competition. The military image transfers perfectly: instead of going around a physical army, you go around someone's position, strategy, or defense in a clever, non-direct way.

The feeling of the word is always the same:

  • Someone has a defensive position — a plan, an argument, a strategy, a stronghold.
  • Instead of confronting it head-on (which may fail), you find a way around it.
  • You end up in a position of advantage that they didn't see coming.

In politics:

"The opposition party outflanked the government by winning the support of rural voters the government had ignored."

The government thought they were safe. The opposition didn't attack them where they were strong — they went around to an area that wasn't being defended.

In business:

"The startup outflanked its larger rival by targeting a younger audience the rival had overlooked."

Instead of competing directly in the same market (a fight they'd lose), the startup went around to a less-defended market and won.

In a debate or argument:

"She outflanked his argument by bringing up a fact he had never considered."

He thought he had a strong position. She didn't argue against his main point directly — she came at him from a surprising angle that exposed a weakness.

In sports:

"The winger outflanked the defender by sprinting along the edge of the field."

Instead of going through the defender, she went around him on the outside.

Several words might seem similar — like bypass, circumvent, or outmaneuver — but "outflank" carries specific qualities that make it unique:

1. It's competitive. You don't "outflank" an empty room. There is always an opponent involved — someone you are trying to beat or overcome.

2. It implies cleverness and strategy. Outflanking is never accidental. It suggests that you thought about your opponent's position carefully, found a gap or a weak side, and deliberately exploited it. It's a smart move, not a brute-force one.

3. It implies going around, not through. This is crucial. When you outflank someone, you are specifically avoiding their strongest point and finding a route to the side. You don't overpower them head-on — you outsmart them by choosing a better angle.

4. It results in a position of advantage. Outflanking isn't just about moving sideways — the whole point is that you end up better positioned than your opponent as a result.
The Grammar: How to Use It

"Outflank" is a transitive verb, which means it always needs an object — the person or thing being outflanked.

  • ✅ "She outflanked her competitor." (correct — has an object)
  • ❌ "She outflanked." (incorrect — missing an object)

Common forms:

  • Present: outflank / outflanks → "He outflanks his rivals regularly."
  • Past: outflanked → "They outflanked the opposition."
  • Continuous: outflanking → "She is outflanking their strategy."
The Single Sentence to Remember It

If you had to compress the entire meaning of "outflank" into one mental image, remember this:

Instead of hitting the wall, you go around it — and you end up on the other side while your opponent is still staring at where you used to be.

That is what it means to outflank someone.
